ARTICLE IN PRESS Dance therapy in rehabilitation: a two-decade bibliometric analysis (2000 - 2024) Abstract Dance therapy integrates movement and dance, enhances emotional, cognitive, and physical health, making it a valuable rehabilitation tool. Dance therapy has been applied to clinical populations, addressing depression, Parkinson’s disease, and dementia. Despite its expanding application in rehabilitation settings, to our knowledge, no prior study has systematically mapped the bibliometric landscape of dance therapy in rehabilitation. This study performed the first longitudinal bibliometric S analysis focused on dance therapy in rehabilitation, identifying key research areas, emerging trends, and S the evolution of dance therapy's role in rehabilitation. E R P A systematic search was conducted in the Web of Science Core Collection, yielding 1,356 publications N from January 1, 2000, to December 31, 2024. Bibliometric analyses were performed using VOSviewer, I bibliometrix in R, Scimago, and CiteSpace to construct collaborative networks, perform co-occurrence E analyses, and visualize thematic evoluLtions. The annual number of publications increased significantly C over the study period, from 3 studies in 2000 to 188 in 2024, achieving a compound annual growth rate I T of 19.34%. A total of 26,254 citations were received by 2024, an average of 19.4 citations per publication. R The United States, UAnited Kingdom, and China emerged as the most productive countries, with notable collaborations among leading institutions such as the University of Haifa and Drexel University. Keyword analyses revealed research hotspots including the efficacy of dance therapy for improving mental health (depression, anxiety), and quality of life through dance therapy, Parkinson’s disease, and neurodegenerative diseases. Emerging trends indicate a growing focus on complementary and alternative medicine approaches within the field. This study shows, dance therapy in rehabilitation has experienced substantial growth and diversification of research themes. Enhanced interdisciplinary cooperation and further exploration of emerging trends are recommended to advance the integration of dance therapy into comprehensive rehabilitation strategies. Introduction Dance therapy is a therapeutic approach that uses movement and dance to improve emotional, cognitive, and physical health, as well as to promote social integration (Veronese et al., 2017). The latest definition of dance therapy by The American Dance Therapy Association (ADTA) is “the psychotherapeutic use of dance, movement, body awareness, and embodied communication to foster healing and well-being for all individuals.”(The American Dance Therapy Association, 2025) S Beyond its functional benefits, dance therapy represents a unique intersection of artistic practice and S health intervention, rooted in embodied experience and culturalEly embedded forms of communication. R Since the establishment of the ADTA in 1966,(Devereaux et al., 2016) dance therapy has been applied P to various clinical populations. As an adjunctive treatm ent in rehabilitation, dance therapy is increasingly N employed to help regulate bodily functions, facilitate emotional adjustment, support disease I treatment.(Acolin, 2016) E L C Research has demonstrated its effectiveness to varying degrees of evidence quality in treating a wide I T range of conditions, such as depression,(Meekums et al., 2015) dementia,(Karkou & Meekums, 2017; R Ruiz-Muelle & LópeAz-Rodríguez, 2019) Parkinson’s disease (Ernst et al., 2023), and frailty. For example, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that dance therapy can reduce symptoms of depression by promoting positive emotional expression and stimulate the release of endorphins, improving mood,(Karkou et al., 2019) In individuals with Parkinson’s disease, dance therapy has been shown to improve motor function, balance, and coordination, thereby increasing physical mobility and quality of life with a relatively high level of quality evidence.(Barnish & Barran, 2020; Pinto et al., 2024) In older adults, dance therapy has been used to improve strength, balance, and gait, helping to reduce the risk of falls.(Lazo Green et al., 2024; Mattle et al., 2020) In patients with dementia, the certainty of evidence remains low (Karkou et al., 2023), contrasting evidence has been reported, while some research has found dance therapy to enhance executive and cognitive functions, such as memory and attention, others have found limited or no significant effects on global cognitive outcomes. Discussion The findings of this study provide a comprehensive overview of the evolving landscape of dance therapy in rehabilitation, offering insights into its growth, key contributors, and emerging trends. Our analysis reveals that research on dance therapy in rehabilitation has been ongoing for over two decades, with a notable surge in publications over the past five years. Research in this field has been led by Western nations. In recent years, however, there has been a marked rise in contributions from emerging economies, particularly across East Asia and Latin America. For example, China and Brazil have significantly increased their research output. China's increasing involvement may be linked to a growing emphasis on integrating alternative therapies into their healthcare system,(Zhou et al., 2024) with research indicating a rising demand for rehabilitation services, ARTICLE IN PRESS with approximately 33% of the population requiring some form of rehabilitation. (Tian et al., 2025) Similar, though more modest trends have been observed in Brazil, where recent research suggests a growing interest in cultural dance therapy programs across Latin America. (Acarón et al., 2023) However, it must be stated that while significant growth has been achieved, further development of the fields is needed in these countries. In China dance therapy in rehabilitation still faces several challenges, including the need for standardized training, greater academic involvement and the establishment of local dance therapy governing bodies.(Zhou et al., 2019) In Latin America, comparable struggles have been found, particularly regarding the lack of university-based accredited training programs, limited professional visibility, and insufficient peer support networks.(Acarón et al., 2023) Altogether, these findings indicate that interest in dance therapy in rehabilitation is not only global but also expanding into regions that have S traditionally been underrepresented in rehabilitation research. While significant growth has been S achieved, further development is essential to address existing chEallenges and enhance the effectiveness R of dance therapy’s use in rehabilitation within developing nations. First, our search was limited to a single database, excluding non- WOSCC databases may restrict the data available, particularly for the fields of arts and humanities.(Liu et al., 2024) However，WOSCC is considered the most comprehensive database with comparatively extensive data. Furthermore, bibliometric studies often favor WOSCC to avoid data errors that can arise from combining sources. Future research could benefit from incorporating additional databases, such as Scopus, to enhance the breadth of the data. Second, only English-language articles were included, which may have led to the exclusion of relevant research published in other languages and could potentially introduce language bias, however, it would be unlikely to change the conclusions of our research (Nussbaumer-Streit et al., 2020). Third, this study did not include grey literature or unpublished trials, which may have led to an underrepresentation of emerging or non-indexed research in the field. Fourth, ARTICLE IN PRESS co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence analyses may not fully capture the extent of collaboration or the true thematic scope of the field. Some authors may have contributed to multiple studies without being identified as core authors, and keyword analysis may miss emerging trends if different terminologies or classifications are used by authors. Fifth, while we included GDP as a measure of economic context, it is important to recognize that economic metrics alone may not fully reflect the diverse factors influencing regional research capacity. (Azizan, 2024a) Relying solely on GDP could overlook variations in scientific infrastructure, funding mechanisms, and local research priorities that also shape research output. Sixth, we excluded research from 2025 to avoid the inclusion of ongoing research, however it must be acknowledged that recent hotspots from 2025 may have been missed. Sixth, in some fields with small author pools, there may be some self-citation effects that exaggerate the influence of studies. However, S for influential authors and articles, the high citation count will far exceed the number of articles published S from related authors pools. Finally, this study did not include AEltmetrics or patents citation analyses, R which could provide insights into the translational and societal impact of research. Future studies could P incorporate these metrics to better assess the real-world influence of scholarly work in this field. JSON: Name: dance_therapy_bibliometric_pipeline Title: Longitudinal bibliometric and network analysis of research trends and collaborations in dance therapy for rehabilitation (2000–2024) Short Hypothesis: Publications featuring international and interdisciplinary co-authorship have higher citation impact (citations per year) than publications lacking international or interdisciplinary co-authorship in the field of dance therapy in rehabilitation between 2000 and 2024. Related Work: Existing work comprises clinical systematic reviews and meta-analyses assessing efficacy of dance interventions for depression, Parkinson’s disease, dementia and falls, and isolated bibliometric studies applied to other rehabilitation subdomains (e.g., frailty, sensor-based fall prevention). Prior bibliometric approaches typically use single-database cross-sectional snapshots, simple volume and citation counts, and descriptive co-authorship maps. Limitations in prior approaches include: reliance on single-source indexing (coverage and language bias), scarce normalization for economic/population factors, limited temporal dynamics (few studies model growth rates or citation bursts longitudinally), insufficient use of multivariate models linking network structure to impact, weak author disambiguation and provenance tracking, and lack of sensitivity analyses (database choice, inclusion criteria, document type). There is also limited integration of bibliometric indicators with downstream translational signals (altmetrics, clinical guideline citations or patient-outcome linkage). Abstract: This pipeline formalizes a reproducible longitudinal bibliometric and network-analysis workflow to map research production, collaboration patterns, and impact drivers in dance therapy applied to rehabilitation (2000–2024). Using comprehensive indexed records and standardized preprocessing, the pipeline constructs co-authorship, institutional, country and keyword networks, computes temporal metrics (annual counts, CAGR, citation bursts), and quantifies interdisciplinarity and international collaboration. The primary contribution is an inferential component that tests whether international and interdisciplinary collaboration predict higher citation impact while controlling for confounders (publication age, journal outlet, number of authors, and country-level economic indicators). Secondary outputs include normalized country productivity (per GDP and per capita), core journal identification by Bradford zones, and interactive network visualizations. Expected outcomes are (1) robust, reproducible estimates of growth and hotspots in dance-therapy rehabilitation research, (2) quantified relationships between collaboration structure and scholarly impact, and (3) sensitivity analyses demonstrating the effect of database choice and normalization on conclusions. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = Web of Science Core Collection exports (plain text) with query: TS=(Dance therapy OR Dance movement therapy) AND TS=(Rehabilitat* OR Recover* OR Heal* OR Restorat* OR Recuperat* OR Restitut* OR Recondition* OR Reintegrat* OR Readaptat* OR Remediat* OR Convalescence OR treat* OR therap*) NOT TS=(neuroblastoma OR dancing eyes OR opsoclonus-myoclonus OR dancing eye syndrome OR kinsbourne syndrome OR paraneoplastic syndrome OR rituximab); date range 2000-01-01 to 2024-12-31; document types: Article, Review; language: English. Supplementary datasets for sensitivity: Scopus and PubMed exports with equivalent queries. Preprocessing: deduplicate by DOI; author name disambiguation using rule-based + ORCID where available; affiliation harmonization; map journal categories to ASJC/WoS subject fields. Network construction: co-authorship (authors, institutions, countries), co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and keyword co-occurrence. Baselines: (B1) raw publication and citation counts (no normalization), (B2) single-database WoS only, (B3) descriptive network centrality metrics only. Primary evaluation metrics: annual publication counts, CAGR, total citations, citations per year, H-index (field subset), network metrics (degree, betweenness, eigenvector centrality, modularity, density), interdisciplinarity score (Shannon entropy of journal categories per paper), international_coauthorship (binary), total_link_strength (TLS), and citation burst strength. Statistical tests and models: group comparison of citation impact between publications with and without international/interdisciplinary co-authorship using Mann-Whitney U and effect sizes; negative binomial or zero-inflated negative binomial regression predicting citation counts (dependent) with predictors: international_coauth (binary), interdisciplinarity_score, number_of_authors, journal_impact_factor, publication_age (years), open_access (binary), country_GDP_per_capita (of corresponding author), and document_type; include cluster-robust SE at journal level. Time-series analyses: LOESS smoothing of annual counts, Prais-Winsten regression for trend, change-point detection for bursts. Network dynamics: compute yearly sliding-window networks (window=3 years) and measure temporal change in centrality and modularity. Burst detection: CiteSpace parameters time-slice=1, g-index/k-core per protocol. Ablation studies: (A1) exclude reviews vs include; (A2) WoS only vs WoS+Scopus; (A3) normalization by GDP/population vs raw counts; (A4) regressions with vs without interdisciplinarity score. Robustness: bootstrap (n=1000) confidence intervals for regression coefficients and network metric distributions; repeat analyses excluding last two years to account for citation lag. Significance: two-sided tests, FDR correction for multiple comparisons. Tools: Bibliometrix (R), VOSviewer, CiteSpace, Gephi; all scripts version-controlled and parameterized for reproducibility. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Data coverage bias: WoS may underrepresent arts/humanities and non-English literature; results may change when Scopus or regional indexes are included. 2) Author disambiguation errors: homonyms and affiliation changes can distort co-authorship networks and centrality measures. 3) Citation lag and windowing: recent publications have fewer citations, biasing impact measures; time-slice choices affect burst and trend detection. 4) Confounding and causality: observed associations between collaboration structure and citations may be confounded (e.g., high-impact journals attract international teams); regression cannot fully establish causation. 5) Self-citation and field-size effects: self-citations and varying community sizes across regions inflate local impact metrics. 6) Normalization sensitivity: GDP and population normalization depend on chosen year and may misrepresent funding landscapes. 7) Reproducibility/legal: vendor data licenses may restrict sharing of raw records; full replication may require institutional access. 8) Scalability and compute: constructing dense temporal networks and bootstrapping regressions can require substantial memory/CPU for large combined datasets. 9) Generalization limits: findings apply to indexed scholarly output and may not reflect outreach, clinical adoption, or patient outcomes. 10) Metric interpretation: bibliometric indicators capture scholarly attention, not clinical effectiveness or translational value.
